reading.body:
AI adoption in US churches is not tracked by any official census; it is measured by a patchwork of research firms, faith-tech platforms, and academic institutes.

The pattern is measurement by survey and platform rather than by census. Barna Group runs the closest thing to sector-wide survey data, Gloo reports deployment across thousands of US churches, and Hartford and Pew add congregational and public attitude data. Census BTOS includes religious and civic organisations in its service-sector series, but no better official measure exists yet.

This matters for AI because adoption in churches is real but diffuse, and every tradition is writing its own guidance. The data does not say how many congregations actually use AI, how much compute that use requires, or what it means for power demand. It also does not give a single adoption rate, because none exists.

summary: No single body tracks AI adoption across America's hundreds of thousands of congregations - coverage comes from research firms, faith-tech platforms, and academic institutes, and this page names them rather than pretending a census exists. Sermon research, translation, accessibility, and administration are the working uses; every tradition is writing its own guidance.

analysis.body:
The only official adoption figure in this material comes from the Census Bureau. In its Business Trends and Outlook Survey, 15.0% of firms in Other services, the NAICS 81 grouping that includes religious organizations, answered yes to a question about whether the business used AI in the last two weeks, up from 13.7% in the prior period. The survey first asked about AI in September 2023. That number describes a broad service-sector bucket rather than congregations specifically, and it is the closest thing to a measured figure the sources offer.

What congregations actually do with AI is described mainly by the sector's own platform and research organizations. Gloo, which the curated points describe as used by thousands of US churches, says it delivers values-aligned models, developer tools and benchmarks for faith-based organizations, and that AI is a foundational capability across its platform to support mission effectiveness, preserve relational ministry and create practical value across the faith and flourishing ecosystem. Its AI Studio offers API-first support for inference, RAG and assistant workflows with dynamic selection of the appropriate model for every request. This page's own scope note frames the sector's use as sermon prep, administration and pastoral limits across hundreds of thousands of congregations.

Barna Group is the research organization the material points to for national studies. It describes itself as a Christian research organization providing data and insights on trends affecting faith, culture and ministry, and its published work includes The State of Pastors, Volume 2, a report on how pastors are navigating post-pandemic life and ministry, along with a webcast on six trends shaping the future of pastoral leadership and a podcast hosted by pastors Glenn Packiam, Rich Villodas and Sharon Hodde Miller. The Hartford Institute for Religion Research, which has a 45 year history of providing accurate research on churches and congregational life, is the other survey body named here. The harvested excerpts from both do not report AI adoption percentages, so no congregation-level figure can be quoted from them.

The ethics side is organized around two institutions. AI and Faith describes itself as a global network of faith leaders and communities, scholars, technologists, ethicists, educators and partner organizations working under five strategic pillars, and it argues that for the 85 percent of the world's population who claim a religious affiliation, questions about AI are deeply spiritual as well as moral, and that the world's religions offer ancient wisdom that should guide the development and use of AI. The University of Notre Dame's Institute for Ethics and the Common Good, directed by Meghan Sullivan, convenes a multidisciplinary community and promotes interdisciplinary research and policy leadership in AI and technology ethics, with practical models for ethical design, development and deployment.

Notre Dame's material also carries the sharpest caution in this set. Meghan Sullivan, a Catholic philosopher at the university who often meets with AI leaders and developers, said many workers in the industry talk very flippantly about job displacement and about AI doing work faster and cheaper, and that some are trying to transcend work and get to a place where they devote all their time to family and hobbies like gardening and crafts. Lily Abadal, a partner at Catholic school consultants Partners in Mission, a professor at the University of South Florida and a faculty fellow with a Notre Dame project called DELTA, Human Formation in the Age of AI, said AI awareness has been evolving.

Pew Research Center's religion work is named here as a periodic measure of public and clergy attitudes, but the harvested page shows its religion research topics, including social hostilities involving religion, restrictions on religion, and Catholic and Muslim demographics, and reports no AI-specific findings. Nothing in this material reports ROI, cost savings or deployment outcomes, and nothing in it describes regulation of AI in religious settings. A reader deciding whether to deploy should treat the Census Bureau's 15.0% as a coarse service-sector signal rather than a church figure, look to Barna Group and the Hartford Institute for Religion Research for congregation-level survey work, treat Gloo as the vendor platform that defines what deployment looks like in practice, and read AI and Faith and Notre Dame for the ethical questions the sector's own institutions are asking.

https://ethics.nd.edu/.brief: The University of Notre Dame’s Institute for Ethics and the Common Good, directed by Meghan Sullivan, brings together a multidisciplinary community to address pressing ethical issues, including artificial intelligence and other technology ethics. The institute states that it engages stakeholders to examine real-world challenges and provide practical models for ethical technology design, development, and deployment. Sullivan, a Catholic philosopher, reports that many AI industry workers speak casually about job displacement and the prospect of faster, cheaper work, with some hoping to move beyond work entirely toward family time and hobbies. Lily Abadal, a partner at Partners in Mission and professor at the University of South Florida, notes that awareness of AI has been evolving; she is also a faculty fellow with Notre Dame’s DELTA project on human formation in the age of AI.

https://www.barna.com/.brief: Barna Group describes itself as a Christian research organization that supplies data and insights on trends affecting faith, culture and ministry. Its report, The State of Pastors, Volume 2, takes an in-depth look at how pastors are navigating post-pandemic life and ministry, focused on self-leadership, church leadership and cultural leadership, and a free webcast replay explores six trends shaping the future of pastoral leadership. A podcast hosted by pastors Glenn Packiam, Rich Villodas and Sharon Hodde Miller has them discussing church leadership challenges with guests, covering the health of the pastor and the state of the church. Barna also says young adults are motivated to attend church for a range of personal reasons ,  a search for identity, well-being and growth ,  and that one motivation stands out from all the rest.

https://www.gloo.us/ai.brief: According to Gloo, its AI offering provides models, developer tools, and benchmarks that are aligned with the values of faith-based organizations. The company describes AI as a foundational capability across its platform, intended to support mission effectiveness, preserve relational ministry, and create practical value. Developers using Gloo AI Studio can access connected infrastructure including production environment tools, trusted content, and values-aligned models. The platform also offers API-first support for inference, RAG, and assistant workflows, with dynamic selection of the appropriate model for each request.

https://aiandfaith.org/.brief: AI and Faith describes itself as a global network of faith leaders and communities, scholars, technologists, ethicists, educators and partner organisations working for a future in which artificial intelligence serves humankind, organised under five strategic pillars. It argues that these issues are at root deeply moral, and that for the 85 percent of the world's population who claim a religious affiliation they are also deeply spiritual, so the world's religions offer ancient wisdom that should guide AI's development and use. The organisation says it encourages, connects and equips tech creators, academic researchers, ethicists and theologians to engage with the moral and ethical questions around artificial intelligence and related technologies. It quotes a statement that its goal is to "inject a kind of humility and historicity" into an industry that has often rejected both, calling the project deeply humanistic and one that draws on faith-based, literary, classical and oral traditions. The page also invites tax-deductible donations and signups to a monthly newsletter.
